title: Two languages, one childhood
text: {{1}} was long believed that juggling two languages confused young children, and immigrant families {{2}} once urged to drop the home language {{3}} children might settle better at school. {{4}} the evidence accumulated, however, the advice was quietly withdrawn. Decades of research {{5}} found that bilingual children show {{6}} flexible attention than monolinguals, switch between tasks with less effort, and may develop dementia symptoms years later {{7}} monolinguals do. Two languages, it seems, are not a burden but a gymnasium for the growing brain. A child's two languages are best treated {{8}} two instruments: learning the second sharpens the playing of the first.

gaps.explanation: 'It was long believed that…' — the passive report frame.

The purpose clause after 'so': so that.
